plain_english: Only philosophers are truly free. They alone really live. They don't just enjoy their own lifetime — they add every century to their own. All the years that came before them become theirs.
original_excerpt: The only persons who are really at leisure are those who devote themselves to philosophy: and they alone really live: for they do not merely enjoy their own lifetime, but they annex every century to their own: all the years which have passed before them belong to them.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 14

plain_english: Unless we're completely ungrateful, we should see these great thinkers — the founders of the major schools of philosophy — as having been born for our benefit. They prepared a way of life for us. Thanks to their hard work, we can now see beautiful truths that were once hidden in darkness. We're not locked out of any time period. We can enter any subject we want. If we can find the mental strength to break free from our human limitations, we have a vast stretch of time to explore and enjoy. We can debate with Socrates, question everything with Carneades, find peace with Epicurus, rise above human nature with the Stoics, or reject convention entirely with the Cynics. Since nature lets us connect with every age, why do we stay trapped in our own tiny, fleeting moment? Why not give our whole mind to what is vast and eternal — to what we share with men far better than ourselves?
original_excerpt: Unless we are the most ungrateful creatures in the world, we shall regard these noblest of men, the founders of divine schools of thought, as having been born for us, and having prepared life for us: we are led by the labour of others to behold most beautiful things which have been brought out of darkness into light; we are not shut out from any period, we can make our way into every subject, and, if only we can summon up sufficient strength of mind to overstep the narrow limit of human weakness, we have a vast extent of time wherein to disport ourselves: we may argue with Socrates, doubt with Carneades, repose with Epicurus, overcome human nature with the Stoics, out-herod it with the Cynics. Since Nature allows us to commune with every age, why do we not abstract ourselves from our own petty fleeting span of time, and give ourselves up with our whole mind to what is vast, what is eternal, what we share with better men than ourselves?
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 14

plain_english: Think about those people who rush around the city making social calls. They worry themselves sick and drive everyone else crazy too. They chase after their obsession completely. They visit every powerful person's house every single day. They never pass up an open door. They peddle their fake friendly greetings to houses of all different types. But after all this effort, how few people do they actually get to see in such a huge city filled with so many different desires and interests? How many people will be too lazy, too self-indulgent, or just too rude to let them in? How many will torment them for ages, then rush past them pretending to be in a hurry? How many will avoid coming out through their main entrance hall (crowded with clients) and sneak out the back door instead? As if tricking a visitor isn't ruder than just refusing to see them in the first place! And how many are half-asleep and stupid from last night's drinking? Even after their servant whispers the poor visitor's name for the thousandth time, they can barely manage to return his greeting. The best they can do is an insulting yawn through half-open lips. This miserable man broke his own sleep just to attend to theirs.
original_excerpt: Those who gad about in a round of calls, who worry themselves and others, after they have indulged their madness to the full, and crossed every patron's threshold daily, leaving no open door unentered, after they have hawked about their interested greetings in houses of the most various character,—after all, how few people are they able to see out of so vast a city, divided among so many different ruling passions: how many will be moved by sloth, self-indulgence, or rudeness to deny them admittance: how many, after they have long plagued them, will run past them with feigned hurry? how many will avoid coming out through their entrance-hall with its crowds of clients, and will escape by some concealed backdoor? as though it were not ruder to deceive their visitor than to deny him admittance!—how many, half asleep and stupid with yesterday's debauch, can hardly be brought to return the greeting of the wretched man who has broken his own rest in order to wait on that of another, even after his name has been whispered to them for the thousandth time, save by a most offensive yawn of his half-opened lips.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 14

plain_english: The people who are truly living right are those who spend time every day with Zeno, Pythagoras, Democritus, and the other great teachers of virtue — with Aristotle and Theophrastus. None of these men will be "too busy" for you. None will send you away without making you feel happier and more at peace with yourself. None will let you leave empty-handed. And here's the best part: anyone can enjoy their company, day or night.
original_excerpt: We may truly say that those men are pursuing the true path of duty, who wish every day to consort on the most familiar terms with Zeno, Pythagoras, Democritus, and the rest of those high priests of virtue, with Aristotle and with Theophrastus. None of these men will be "engaged," none of these will fail to send you away after visiting him in a happier frame of mind and on better terms with yourself, none of them will let you leave him empty-handed: yet their society may be enjoyed by all men, and by night as well as by day.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 14
